title: Long-memory stitchbook — tinker notes
content:
Notes to self: long-memory stitching experiments and quick reading summaries.

Context and motivation:
- Trying to get reliable long-context behavior for product-style conversations (20k+ effective context) without blowing latency or memory.
- Tradeoff space I've been thinking about: local KV caching (low latency, limited capacity) vs episodic checkpoints (higher recall, more compute to restore) vs retrieval (index + embedding lookup, variable latency).
- Want a hybrid that: 1) preserves recent conversational state cheaply; 2) allows jump-to earlier episodes when needed; 3) yields graceful degradation when a heavy restore would exceed latency SLO.

Quick paper hits (skim notes):
- Paper A (arXiv 2403.12345): sticky tokens + compressed episodic checkpoints. Interesting compression scheme using local PCA on KV vectors to reduce checkpoint size by 6x. Notes: PCA needs offline compute; check stability with quantized kernels. Hypothesis: PCA plus 4-bit quantization might still preserve retrieval quality for prompts under 200 tokens.
- Blog post: "Memory-first prompt engineering" (internal link): practical heuristics for sketching sparse summaries of episodes rather than storing full KV. Takeaway: store canonicalized bullet anchors aligned to retrieval keys helps matching later.
- Conference talk (MLSys 2026): real-time KV eviction policies tuned to sequence-length histograms. Key idea: prioritize finger-printed keys (tokens occurring across multiple sessions) for hot-preservation.

Key ideas / heuristics to try:
- Stitched-history representation: keep dense KV for last N=1024 tokens, store 2–3 compressed episodic checkpoints covering previous chunks of 10k tokens. On retrieval, fast path: match by anchor embeddings -> if high confidence, inject checkpoint's reconstructed KV prefix; else fall back to retrieval-of-documents.
- Soft-fallback policy: if checkpoint restore would add > 40ms p99, return a heuristic summary + model prompt that asks model to infer missing context. (Intent: keep SLOs and accept slightly degraded quality occasionally.)
- Anchor embedding engineering: use pooled embeddings from message boundaries, normalized, stored in in-memory LRU index for low-latency nearest neighbor. Keep ~8k anchors in RAM per GPU host.

Microbench sketch (what I ran last week):
- Setup: MPT-30B-like model on single A100, KV-store simulated as float16 tensors. Baseline: naive restore (copy full KV of 50k tokens) -> p50 180ms, p95 420ms.
- Compressed checkpoint (PCA 32-dim + 8-bit quantize): p50 95ms, p95 150ms, quality drop measured by perplexity on held prompts: +6% relative.
- Anchor match + selective restore: p50 60ms, p95 110ms, quality drop varied by prompt class (FAQ-style prompts almost unchanged; code-reasoning prompts worse).

Open questions / things to probe next:
- How much does quantization of compressed checkpoints amplify hallucination risk for reasoning tasks? Need targeted eval set (create 200-case reasoning probe).
- Cost model: what is RAM vs network transfer tradeoff for multi-host setups? If we keep anchors in host RAM and checkpoints in shared object store, need precise numbers for cloud infra (estimate egress + object store latency vs single large restore).
- Can we improve anchor embeddings by distillation from the last-layer logits rather than standard sentence-BERT? Quick idea: distilled anchor that points to likely model executions rather than semantic content. Worth a small ablation.

Experiment plan (next two sprints):
- Sprint A (2 weeks): build anchor index prototype + selective restore path. Implement two match thresholds (0.75 high-confidence -> full checkpoint restore; 0.5 -> inject bullet summary; else -> no restore). Measure p50/p95 and quality on small eval sets.
- Sprint B (2 weeks): add compressed checkpoint pipeline (PCA + 4-bit quantize), integrate with selective restore. Run batch of 1k synthetic sessions with mixed QA/code prompts. Track token-level accuracy and hallucination rate.
- Metrics to record: latency p50/p95, CPU/GPU overhead, storage per session, quality delta (relative to full-KV restore), and false-positive restores (restore when not needed).

Prototype TODOs (implementation notes):
- [ ] Make a lightweight anchor extractor: boundary detection + mean pooling over last hidden states (configurable layer).
- [ ] Implement in-memory ring index with approximate NN (HNSW small candidate set ~32). Reuse existing disk-backed index service if possible.
- [ ] PCA compressor: schedule offline compute job for chunked KVs; explore learning a small autoencoder (2-layer) instead of PCA for non-linear compressions.
- [ ] Create small eval harness: 200 FAQ, 200 code-understanding, 200 multi-turn story chaining prompts. Keep the harness reproducible and check into repo.

Risk notes & mitigations:
- Risk: false positives (restoring wrong checkpoint) cause strong degradation. Mitigation: conservative thresholding + inject short summary instead of raw KV until confidence validated.
- Risk: operational complexity if checkpoints are stored across hosts. Mitigation: start with single-host experiments; if multi-host needed, prefer object-store with signed URLs and prefetch heuristics.

Random heuristics (brain dump):
- If a session is > 50k tokens but has < 10 anchor matches in last 30k tokens, probably topic drift — consider summarization-based archiving rather than reconstructing full history.
- Keep a "session health" score in metadata: last-response-entropy, anchor-density, retrieval-hit-rate — use this to decide canary restore policies.

Short list of references to bookmark (for myself):
- arXiv:2403.12345 (episodic checkpoints + compression)
- internal blog: memory-first prompts (link in linked_artifacts)
- MLSys 2026 talk: KV eviction policies (slides)

Next actions today:
- Draft Linear ticket for anchor + index prototype (LINEAR-4567). Add acceptance criteria: reproducible benchmark script and p95 latency below 140ms for selective-restore path on toy host.
- Ping Kenji for help wiring the HNSW index; ask Mira to compile the reasoning-probe dataset samples.

End of current notes. Keep this as the experimental "stitchbook" — add raw logs and microbench CSVs here as I run tests (I'll paste results under a new header with timestamps).

-- Jordan
